Trace: p=&a, q=&b, r=&a. After `p = q; q = &c;` p points at b, q at c, r still at a. `*p = *q` sets b=3; `*r = *q + 1` sets a=4; `*q = 5` sets c=5. So *p=b=3, *q=c=5, *r=a=4. `*numbers` is numbers[0]=10 and `*(numbers+2)` is numbers[2]=30.
questions.grading: Verified by compiling and running. Two marks per line (5 lines). Line 3 and line 4 are the ones students usually get wrong: the common mistake is forgetting that after `p = q`, p points at b (not a), so `*p = *q` changes b, not a. Another common error is `*(numbers+2)` = 12 (adding 2 to the value) or 20 (off by one). Award a line's marks only if all three values on it are right, but if an early mistake is carried consistently into lines 3–4, give partial credit (1 of 2) for lines that are correct given the student's earlier values. Exact spacing/punctuation doesn't matter.

Trace: p=&y, q=&z, r=&y. After `q = p; p = &x;` q points at y, p at x, r at y. `*q = *p + 2` sets y=6; `*p = *r * 2` sets x=12 (r points at y, now 6); `r = &z` then `*r = *q - 1` sets z=5. So *p=x=12, *q=y=6, *r=z=5. Line 5: `*(values+3)` is values[3]=12, `*values + 3` is values[0]+3=6, `values[5]`=18.
questions.grading: Verified by compiling and running. Two marks per line. Common errors: using y's old value 7 in `*p = *r * 2` (giving 14), forgetting that `r = &z` re-points r before the last assignment, and reading `*values + 3` as `*(values + 3)` (precedence: `*` binds tighter than `+`, so it is 3+3=6, not 12). Award a line's marks only if all values on it are right; give 1 of 2 for later lines that are consistent with an earlier error.

questions.prompt:
**Question 4 (10 points): I/O and Strings**

Write a complete C program that reads a text file and decides if the lines in the file are in alphabetical order. The program should take one command line argument, the name of the input file. (Save time by assuming there will be exactly one argument.) If the lines of the input file are in order, the program should print a confirmation message to the standard output and exit successfully. If the lines are not in order, it should print a message to the standard output identifying the first pair of lines that are out of order and exit with a failure status.

Your program should compare lines as strings, in dictionary order with a case-sensitive comparison. (Hint: use the `strcmp` function.) It's okay if the input file contains duplicate lines. Lines may contain spaces.

If any line in the input file contains more than 100 characters, your program should immediately write an error message and exit with a failure status.

You may assume that there is at least one line in the input file.

Besides looking for lines over 100 characters long, the only I/O error you need to check for is not being able to open the input file. In that case, your program should write an error message and exit with a failure status.

Here is a transcript showing the correct behavior (assuming that your program is called `ordered`):

```
-------$ cat good
apple
banana
grape
grape
orange
-------$ ordered good
lines in input are in order
$: cat bad
apple
grape
banana
peach
orange
-------$ ordered bad
lines out of order:
  grape
  banana
-------$
```

(Exam instructions: you don't need to bother with `#include`s for libraries; you may use any C library functions.)
questions.grading:
Any correct approach is fine. Essentials: open the file named by `argv[1]` with `fopen` and check for NULL (error message, failure exit); read line by line (`fgets` is the natural choice; `getline` or reading char by char are also fine); detect lines longer than 100 characters (with `fgets`, a buffer of at least 102 chars and checking the length after removing the newline, or checking that a newline was read); remember the previous line (`strcpy` into a second buffer, or swap two buffers) and compare with `strcmp(prev, curr) > 0`; print both lines of the first out-of-order pair and exit with a failure status (`exit(EXIT_FAILURE)`, `exit(1)`, or `return 1` from main); otherwise print a confirmation and exit successfully.

Common mistakes that lose marks: comparing pointers with `<` or `==` instead of `strcmp`; storing only a pointer to the buffer as the "previous line" (it is overwritten by the next `fgets`, so prev and curr are always equal); a buffer of exactly 100 chars, which cannot hold a 100-char line plus the newline and '\0' and then mis-splits lines; not stripping the newline, which is mostly harmless for comparison but wrong if the last line has no newline ("zoo" vs "zoo\n") — minor deduction at most; treating duplicate lines as out of order (`>= 0` instead of `> 0`); forgetting to exit with a failure status. The paper says `#include`s may be omitted. Error messages may go to stdout or stderr (stderr is better). Exact wording of messages doesn't matter.

rubric.item: Opens argv[1] with fopen and on failure prints an error and exits with a failure status
Reads the file one line at a time in a correct loop (e.g. while (fgets(buf, size, f) != NULL)) with a suitably sized buffer
Detects a line longer than 100 characters, prints an error and exits with a failure status
Keeps a copy of the previous line (strcpy or buffer swap, not just a pointer to the same buffer) and compares with strcmp, allowing duplicates
On the first out-of-order pair prints both lines to stdout and exits with a failure status
If all lines are in order, prints a confirmation and exits successfully

questions.prompt:
Write a complete C program that reads a text file and decides if the lines in the file are sorted by length, shortest first (each line is no longer than the line after it). The program should take one command line argument, the name of the input file. (Save time by assuming there will be exactly one argument.) If the lines are sorted by length, the program should print a confirmation message to the standard output and exit successfully. If not, it should print a message to the standard output identifying the line numbers and contents of the first pair of lines that are out of order, and exit with a failure status.

Lines of equal length are fine in any order. Lines may contain spaces. The length of a line does not include its newline character.

If any line in the input file contains more than 80 characters, your program should immediately write an error message that includes the line number and exit with a failure status.

You may assume that there is at least one line in the input file.

Besides looking for lines over 80 characters long, the only I/O error you need to check for is not being able to open the input file. In that case, your program should write an error message and exit with a failure status.

Here is a transcript showing the correct behavior (assuming that your program is called `bylength`):

```
$ cat short
to
cat
frog
frog
horses
$ bylength short
lines are sorted by length
$ cat mixed
a
bee
at
zebra
$ bylength mixed
lines 2 and 3 are out of order:
  bee
  at
$
```
questions.grading:
Essentials: `fopen(argv[1], "r")` with a NULL check (error + failure exit); a line-by-line read loop (`fgets` with a buffer of at least 82 chars, `getline`, or char-by-char); remove or account for the newline when measuring length (a line that ends with '\n' and one at end of file without it must be treated the same); count line numbers; error (with line number) and failure exit for a line over 80 chars; remember the previous line's contents (or at least its length plus a copy of its text, since the text must be printed) and compare lengths with `strlen`; print both line numbers and both lines for the first out-of-order pair and exit with failure; otherwise print a confirmation and exit successfully.

Common mistakes: comparing strings with `strcmp` instead of comparing lengths; counting the newline in the length (makes the last line, if it lacks a newline, look one shorter); treating equal lengths as out of order; keeping only a pointer to the read buffer as the previous line; off-by-one line numbers. Message wording does not matter.

rubric.item: Opens argv[1] and handles fopen failure with an error message and failure exit
Correct line-by-line read loop with a big enough buffer, tracking line numbers
Detects a line over 80 characters (newline not counted), prints error with the line number, exits with failure
Keeps the previous line's text and compares lengths with strlen, allowing equal lengths
Prints the line numbers and contents of the first out-of-order pair and exits with failure
Prints a confirmation and exits successfully when sorted

questions.grading:
Essentials: handle `list == NULL` and `list->next == NULL` by returning 0 *before* dereferencing anything else; save a pointer to the second node and its `data` before freeing; relink `list->next = second->next` (so the third node, or NULL, becomes the second); `free` the removed node; return the saved value. Accept `(*list).next`, a temporary for the third node, or any equivalent ordering as long as nothing is read from the node after `free`.

Common mistakes: reading `second->data` or `second->next` after `free(second)` (use after free: lose 2); freeing the wrong node (e.g. `free(list)`) or not freeing at all (memory leak: lose 2); `list->next = list->next` or otherwise losing the rest of the list; dereferencing `list->next->next` without checking that `list->next` is non-NULL; returning the deleted node's pointer instead of its data. Note the function cannot (and need not) change the caller's `list` variable because the first node is never deleted.

rubric.item: Returns 0 without doing anything for an empty list and for a one-element list (checks before dereferencing)
Gets a pointer to the second node and saves its data value
Relinks the first node to the third node (list->next = second->next), keeping the rest of the list intact
Frees the deleted node, and only after everything needed from it has been read
Returns the deleted value; correct header and no other errors

questions.grading:
Essentials: return 0 for `list == NULL` or `list->next == NULL`; walk to the **second-last** node (loop while `prev->next->next != NULL`, or keep a trailing `prev` pointer behind a `curr` pointer); save the last node's data; set the second-last node's `next` to NULL; `free` the last node; return the saved value.

Common mistakes: walking to the last node itself and then having no way to set the previous node's `next` to NULL (leaves a dangling pointer in the list: lose 2–4); reading the data after `free`; not freeing (leak); not setting `next` to NULL; dereferencing `list->next->next` before checking for a one-element list. Any correct traversal style (while/for, two pointers) is fine.

rubric.item: Returns 0 without changes for an empty or one-element list
Correctly finds the second-last node (or tracks a previous pointer)
Saves the last node's data before freeing
Sets the second-last node's next to NULL and frees the last node
Returns the deleted value; no use after free or other errors
